# A Map of AI-for-Architecture Work {#sec-appendix-b-ai-for-architecture-map}

::: {.abstract}
This map consolidates the prior body of AI-for-architecture work that Architecture 2.0 builds on. It groups established results into families, maps each family to the principal life-cycle stages where cited work demonstrates activity, and shows how the discipline of an AI-native design system differs from any single method family. This synthesis serves as a positioning statement rather than an exhaustive literature survey.
:::

Machine learning has appeared in computer architecture for decades. Early work proposed learned in-chip mechanisms and models of architectural design spaces. More recent systems couple learned methods directly to simulators, compilers, and implementation tools. The families below form the foundation on which this work builds; because existing literature already provides comprehensive surveys [@ChenPenneyJimenez2020AIArchitecture], this map offers a positioning aid instead (@tbl-ai-arch-map).

When examined by their underlying claims, most method families fall into three regimes, with each regime supporting a distinct claim. Learned in-chip components occupy the mechanism regime, evaluated against the mechanism's own budget, such as mispredict rate at fixed storage and latency. Learned cost models occupy the design-space-model regime, evaluated by their predictive fidelity against the tool they approximate. Families that participate in the design process itself occupy the third regime. Benchmarks and datasets sit alongside these regimes as supporting evaluation infrastructure. A complete third-regime result must be judged at the level of the architecture study rather than by the generated artifact alone. Confusing these regimes allows a bounded branch-prediction result to be mistaken for evidence that an agent can be trusted with a floorplan.

| **Family of work** | **Representative results** | **Principal life-cycle stages demonstrated** | **Developed in** | **Key sources** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Learned in-chip components** | Perceptron branch predictors and learned prefetchers, where learning is embedded in the mechanism itself and does a bounded tactical job | Implement, Evaluate | @sec-moonshot, @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization | [@JimenezLin2001Perceptron; @ChenPenneyJimenez2020AIArchitecture] |
| **Learned cost models and predictive DSE** | Surrogates and regression models that predict performance and power across a design-space exploration (DSE) environment from cheap features | Explore, Evaluate | @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization | [@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE; @LeeBrooks2006RegressionModeling; @BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer] |

: **The unit of work in Architecture 2.0 is the architecture study and its reviewable claim, not any single family's artifact.** Each row names prior results, the principal life-cycle stages demonstrated by the cited work, and the chapters that develop it. The stage column uses only the six labels defined in @sec-architecture-20-ontology. {#tbl-ai-arch-map tbl-colwidths="[18,32,16,16,18]"}

These families are not mutually exclusive; an agentic design-space search might call a learned cost model, invoke an autoscheduler, and emit RTL within a single study.

The learned in-chip components family carries a unique constraint: a proposed component is viable only when inference fits the mechanism's storage and latency budget. The perceptron predictor illustrates this boundary, operating within a 4\ KB hardware budget and delivering single-cycle predictions [@JimenezLin2001Perceptron].

These families map to distinct regions of @fig-book-composition. Learned components, cost models, and autotuners occupy the intersection of computer architecture and machine learning. Reinforcement learning for physical design and LLM-driven RTL generation occupy the intersection of machine learning and electronic design automation (EDA). Learned models that predict routing hotspots and downstream outcomes extend cost models into physical design [@Kahng2018Machine], enabling fast feedback before running expensive downstream flows. Generated assertions and testbenches span both intersections as candidate verification collateral requiring independent review [@FangEtAl2025AssertLLM; @QiuEtAl2024AutoBench; @KangEtAl2024FVEval]. AgentDSE places tool feedback inside exploration [@WangEtAl2026AgentDSE], while QuArch contributes an Evaluate-stage benchmark of architectural reasoning [@PrakashEtAl2025QuArch].

The stage column in @tbl-ai-arch-map exposes an asymmetry: Explore appears in four rows, Implement in six, and Evaluate in six, yet no row demonstrates Formulate, Interpret Results, or Review and Decide. A complete architecture study must supply those missing responsibilities.

What separates Architecture 2.0 from any single family is the unit of work. Prior literature evaluates bounded outputs: a learned branch predictor modifies one mechanism, a placement agent optimizes one step, and an RTL generator produces one artifact. Architecture 2.0 takes the complete architecture study and its reviewable claim as the fundamental unit of work. The question is not whether a model produced a plausible artifact, but whether the complete loop supports a decision that another architect can inspect, reproduce, and challenge.

## The Latent Architectural Space Map

Machine learning models do not operate directly on raw silicon. They transform discrete hardware artifacts (abstract syntax trees (ASTs), control-data flow graphs (CDFGs), place-and-route netlists, memory traces) into continuous or structured latent representations (@tbl-latent-space-map).

Four paradigms organize this territory: Token and Code Embeddings, Graph and Topological Embeddings, Continuous Surrogate Spaces, and Policy State Spaces. Each paradigm requires an independent physical grounding path to prevent latent hallucinations from corrupting the design loop.

| **Latent Space Paradigm** | **Underlying Representation** | **Search and Inference Mechanism** | **Physical Grounding and Decoupling** | **Primary Latent Failure Mode** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Token and Code Embeddings** | High-dimensional dense vectors derived from LLM activations over Verilog, SystemC, or Triton DSL code | Autoregressive token sampling, temperature decoding, and beam search | Executable compilation via Verilator or Yosys and functional testbenches | **Hallucinated Syntax and Vacuous Syntax:** Generated code looks syntactically plausible but violates ABI, bit-width, or structural invariants. |
| **Graph and Topological Embeddings** | Node and edge embeddings (GNNs, Hypergraphs) capturing spatial connectivity, CDFGs, or netlist floorplans | Node classification, edge prediction, and spatial clustering | Physical place-and-route tools via OpenROAD or Synopsys Innovus and static timing analyzers via OpenSTA | **Nonroutable Clustering:** Surrogates cluster macros optimally in graph space, but extracted physical layouts collapse under severe metal layer congestion. |
| **Continuous Surrogate and DSE Spaces** | Low-dimensional continuous manifolds mapping discrete architecture configurations (cache size, pipeline depth, bus width) to scalar power, performance, and area (PPA) estimates | Bayesian optimization (BO), Gaussian processes, and active learning acquisition functions | Cycle-accurate simulators like SCALE-Sim or gem5 and gate-level signoff via Ansys RedHawk-SC | **Out-of-Distribution Exploitation (Optimizer's Curse):** Optimizers select extreme latent points whose predicted gains are inflated by estimation error rather than by real PPA improvements [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse]. |
| **Policy and Reinforcement State Spaces** | Markov decision process (MDP) state-action vectors representing placement steps, tile schedules, or circuit transformations | deep Q-networks (DQNs), proximal policy optimization (PPO), and Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) | Downstream physical design rule check (DRC) / layout versus schematic (LVS) signoff and formal property checkers via Cadence JasperGold | **Reward Hacking:** The policy maximizes proxy reward functions (e.g., estimated wirelength) by injecting false timing paths or infeasible constraints. |

: **Mapping latent architectural spaces across representation paradigms.** Each paradigm embeds discrete hardware artifacts into continuous or graph-based latent vectors. Physical grounding through independent signoff engines remains mandatory to prevent latent hallucinations from reaching silicon. {#tbl-latent-space-map tbl-colwidths="[18,22,18,20,22]"}

These four paradigms connect to physical reality through structural decoupling, separating latent candidate generation from physical silicon signoff (@fig-latent-architectural-space-map).

![**The Latent Architectural Space Map decouples latent candidate generation from physical silicon signoff.** Machine learning models operate over four core representation paradigms (Token and Code Embeddings, Graph and Topological Embeddings, Continuous Surrogates, and Policy State Spaces). Each paradigm relies on an independent, evaluator-owned physical grounding path (Verilator, OpenROAD, SCALE-Sim, JasperGold) to prevent latent failure modes (Vacuous Syntax, Nonroutable Congestion, Optimizer's Curse, Reward Hacking) from reaching silicon. Verified candidates require human architect and commitment authority signoff across five clean physical signoff checks before tapeout freeze.](images/fig-latent-architectural-space-map){#fig-latent-architectural-space-map width="100%" fig-alt="Architecture diagram showing 4 Latent Space Paradigms at top, an Independent Evaluator-Owned Physical Signoff Barrier in the middle, and Verified Physical Silicon Signoff with Human Architect Commitment Authority at bottom."}

An independent, evaluator-owned physical grounding flow routes latent proposals through deterministic simulation, formal property verification, place-and-route, and static timing signoff across five physical signoff checks:

1. **Static Timing Closure and Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) Integrity:** Verifying that zero setup/hold timing violations exist without unverified false-path or multicycle-path exceptions.
2. **Power Grid and Power-Integrity Verification:** Checking Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 1801 Unified Power Format (UPF) power-domain isolation and confirming dynamic voltage drop (IR-drop) and droop ($di/dt$) remain within noise margins.
3. **Physical Design Rules and Connectivity (DRC / LVS):** Ensuring zero geometrical design rule violations and 100% layout-versus-schematic matching.
4. **Clock and Reset Domain Verification (CDC / RDC):** Formally verifying structural synchronization across asynchronous clock and reset crossings.
5. **Electrothermal and Packaging Feasibility:** Verifying maximum power dissipation, 3D vertical thermal flux, and package pinout limits.

Only physically grounded candidates satisfying all five checks reach the human commitment authority for tapeout authorization.

## Candidates, Not Decisions

In an AI-native design system, model outputs are always candidates, never final decisions. An autoscheduler's proposed schedule supports a performance claim only after measured execution on target hardware. A proposed placement requires downstream place-and-route, timing, power, and congestion checks. Generated RTL requires functional and implementation signoff. The accountable organization retains commitment authority, while verification and implementation owners retain signoff authority for their respective domains.

Candidates can mislead through false confidence or hidden total costs. Generated assertions can pass vacuously while checking nothing that matters, so apparent success is not independent evidence [@BeerEtAl2001Vacuity; @Clarke2018ModelChecking] (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). When evaluating macro-placement methods such as AlphaChip [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement], a fair total-cost comparison must include the pretraining and fine-tuning runs used for the reported design, together with their compute [@ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment]. Neither apparent verification success nor a favorable cost comparison replaces required domain signoff and organizational commitment.

## Survey of Existing AI-Assisted Systems

Public systems through July 2026 demonstrate individual point capabilities across four distinct checking regimes (@tbl-existing-systems):

- **Exact or inexpensive verification.** When candidate solutions admit exact algebraic checks (such as AlphaTensor's matrix multiplication algorithms [@FawziEtAl2022AlphaTensor]) or bounded execution measurements (such as AutoTVM's tensor schedules [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]), automated search can accept or reject candidates reliably. These checks enable efficient local optimization, but do not observe the broader system architecture.
- **Proxy and simulation feedback.** Broader exploration often relies on proxies (such as AlphaChip's wirelength estimates [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment]) or cycle-level simulators (such as ArchGym [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym], Apollo [@yazdanbakhsh2021apollo], and BOOM-Explorer [@BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer]). These methods expand the search space, but their claims remain bounded by the fidelity and blind spots of the underlying simulators.
- **Functional simulation, synthesis, and silicon.** Generated RTL evaluated through functional simulation (VerilogEval [@VerilogEval; @PinckneyEtAl2024RevisitingVerilogEval]) or post-synthesis metrics (RTLLM [@RTLLM]) tests implementation syntax and local quality, but stops short of physical signoff. While Chip-Chat [@BlockloveEtAl2023ChipChat] and Enlightenment-1 [@ChengEtAl2024AutomatedCPU] reached silicon, their flows relied on extensive manual repair or bounded Boolean synthesis rather than closed-loop multi-tool exploration.
- **Human ratings and proprietary reports.** Domain-adapted models (ChipNeMo [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo]), agentic wrappers (ChatEDA [@HeEtAl2024ChatEDA]), and commercial optimization engines (DSO.ai [@Synopsys2023DSOai]) demonstrate productive deployment, but their evaluations lack open matched baselines or complete public signoff data.

Across these systems, each result supports only the specific claim its checks can inspect. No single existing system provides the complete closed-loop architecture capability that the moonshot envisions.

| **System** | **What it establishes** | **The telltale limit** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AlphaTensor [@FawziEtAl2022AlphaTensor] | Learned search improved a fifty-year-old matrix-multiplication count for 4-by-4 matrices modulo 2 | The algebraic construction admits an exact mathematical check, and a single scalar scores it |
| AutoTVM [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM] | Measured search can improve schedules when many candidates run quickly on real hardware | The result covers tensor-program schedules, where failures usually remain safely contained within the tuning run |
| AlphaChip [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment] | A learned policy produces macro placements a production flow accepts | The reward relies on proxy wirelength and congestion, and the matched baseline remains disputed |
| ArchGym [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym] | At equal sample budgets no search algorithm dominates, so the chosen harness and budget ultimately shape the result | Because every candidate is graded by a simulator, the result inherently adopts its fidelity limits |
| Apollo and BOOM-Explorer [@yazdanbakhsh2021apollo; @BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer] | Learned design-space exploration can successfully exploit domain-specific evidence | Apollo adapts learned representations across related accelerator spaces to reduce costly target evaluations; BOOM-Explorer uses an open-source core but depends on commercial tools and pays hours per sample |
| VerilogEval and RTLLM [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM] | RTL generation can be measured on shared benchmark tasks | VerilogEval emphasizes functional simulation; RTLLM adds post-synthesis quality metrics; neither reaches physical signoff |
| Chip-Chat and Enlightenment-1 [@BlockloveEtAl2023ChipChat; @ChengEtAl2024AutomatedCPU] | Generated logic has reached silicon, including a core that successfully boots Linux | One relies on extensive human-guided revision; the other synthesizes a processor from input-output examples with a provable accuracy bound, rather than the full multi-tool system-architecture capability the moonshot poses |
| ChatEDA [@HeEtAl2024ChatEDA] | An agent can plan and invoke a real tool flow directly from stated intent | The benchmark checks tool execution and human-rated request fulfillment on 50 ChatEDA-Bench tasks using a simplified OpenROAD wrapper, lacking independent functional correctness or complete signoff |
| ChipNeMo [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo] | Domain adaptation can improve selected internal engineering tasks | The gains remain task-specific, general models stay stronger on certain subtasks, and outsiders cannot reproduce the proprietary evaluation |
| DSO.ai [@Synopsys2023DSOai] | Learned flow-parameter search has reached 100 vendor-reported commercial tapeouts | The evidence standard remains a vendor report, lacking a public methodology or matched baseline |

: **The strength of each result depends on its scope and how it is evaluated.** Exact, inexpensive checks support strong scoped claims, whereas narrow measurements, proxies, weak baselines, and hidden supporting data, methods, or artifacts all limit what architects can conclude. {#tbl-existing-systems tbl-colwidths="[22,38,40]"}

This table presents scoped claims rather than a definitive ranking of systems. Shared benchmark tasks make it possible to inspect exactly where each claim stops and where further evidence is required.
